day-1.t: Day 1 — What a reader actually looks for

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know who will read your plan and what each one fears
Learn the five questions every reader asks
Plan the document before you write a word

b.v: About 20 minutes. Running example: Sana's Kitchen in Lahore, a frozen samosa and paratha business asking for Rs 15 lakh.

A business plan is not a school project. It is a document that answers the questions a lender or investor will ask, in the order they ask them. Nobody reads it for pleasure. They read it to decide whether to risk money, and they stop reading when they stop believing you.
1) Know your three readers
Each reader has a different fear. Write for the one with the most to lose, and the others will still be satisfied.

v: A bank or microfinance officer = fears that the money will not come back. Wants repayment capacity, collateral, and honest numbers
An investor = fears a small market and a founder who cannot execute. Wants growth and a clear use of funds
A family lender = fears embarrassment and family conflict. Wants a simple plan, a repayment date, and to see that you have thought about failing
All three = hate surprises. A plan that mentions a risk before they ask builds unusual trust

b.v: 2) The five questions, in the reader's order
If your plan answers these five clearly in the first two pages, most readers will keep going. If any one is missing, they usually stop and ask you in person, which is a slower and worse conversation.

Answer all five:|What exactly do you sell, to whom, and why would they choose you?|How much does one sale earn you after its direct costs?|How much do you need to sell each month just to cover your costs?|How much money do you need, what for, and when does it come back?|What could go wrong, and what would you do about it?
3) Plan the document before writing
Ten to fourteen pages is plenty for a small business. More pages do not mean more credibility, they mean more places for the reader to stop believing you.

v: Page 1 = one-page summary. Many readers never go past it
Pages 2 to 4 = the business, the customer, the competition
Pages 5 to 9 = revenue model, unit economics, costs, cash flow, break-even
Pages 10 to 12 = risks, the ask, the use of funds
Appendix = quotations, supplier prices, any letters. Put evidence at the back, not in the argument

b.v: The most common beginner mistake is starting with a proud description of the company and burying the numbers on page nine. The reader decides in ninety seconds. Put the business, the customer and the request for money in the first page, or the rest will not be read.
Practice

Write the five questions on one page and answer each in a single sentence for your own business. Do not open a spreadsheet yet. If you cannot answer question three, that is the topic you must learn before you ask anyone for money.

day-2.t: Day 2 — The one-page summary that opens the door

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write a one-page summary with seven fixed sections
Lead with the request, not the history
Make it readable in three minutes by a busy person

b.v: About 20 minutes. One page, one side, no small fonts.

The one-page summary is the only part of the plan that is guaranteed to be read. If it is vague, the reader assumes the rest is vague too. If it is sharp, they read on with a good opinion already formed, which is worth more than any chart.
1) Seven sections, in this order
The order matters because it follows the reader's curiosity: what is it, who buys it, does it make money, what do you want, what could go wrong.

v: What it is = one sentence. Frozen samosas and parathas, made fresh, sold to shops and homes in Lahore
The customer = who buys, how often, and what they use instead today
The money = price, cost per unit, and the margin in one line
The proof so far = real numbers. Current sales, repeat customers, deposits taken
The ask = Rs 15,00,000, and the four things it buys
The return = when the business repays or pays back, and from what cash
The risk = the one thing most likely to go wrong, and your answer to it

b.v: 2) Write it with numbers, not adjectives
Every adjective you remove makes the page stronger. Replace great, unique, huge and premium with a number the reader can check.

Rewrite three sentences this way:|Bad: we have huge demand from many shops. Good: 11 shops reorder every week, average 22 boxes each|Bad: our margins are excellent. Good: each box sells at Rs 520 and costs Rs 310 to make and deliver, leaving Rs 210|Bad: we need funds for expansion. Good: Rs 15,00,000 for a blast freezer, a delivery bike, packaging stock and six months of working capital

Do not put a five-year projection on the summary page. For a small business it reads as fantasy, and it invites an argument about year four instead of a decision about month one. Twelve months of cash flow is enough at this stage.
3) Make it survive a phone screen
Many readers will open your PDF on a phone, standing in a queue. Design for that and you get read.

v: Body text at 11 point or larger, one column
One table, not four. The most important one is the money
Page numbers and your phone number on every page
Export as PDF, name the file properly: Sana-Kitchen-Plan-2026.pdf

b.v: Practice
Write the seven sections at one page. Then give it to someone who knows nothing about your business and ask them to tell you the ask and the margin. If they cannot, cut words until they can.

day-3.t: Day 3 — Market and competition, told honestly

b.v: Today's goal

v: Size a market from the bottom up, using counts you can defend
Describe competitors without insulting them
State your real advantage in one honest sentence

b.v: About 25 minutes. Bring a notebook and count real shops, not internet figures.

Investors and bankers have read a hundred plans claiming a market of billions. The number is meaningless because nobody can check it and nobody believes it. A bottom-up count of forty shops buying twenty-five boxes a month is small, checkable, and far more persuasive.
1) Count from the bottom up
Start with real customers you can name and multiply. If the answer is small, that is useful information, not a failure. A small market you can actually serve beats a large market you cannot reach.

Build the number for Sana:|List the three areas you can deliver to within 40 minutes|Count grocery and frozen-food shops in those areas: 40 shops|Assume each orders 25 boxes a month once you are established: 40 × 25 = 1,000 boxes|Add direct home customers: 60 regular homes × 3 boxes = 180 boxes|Realistic monthly market you can serve: 1,180 boxes, about Rs 6,13,600 of sales at Rs 520 a box|Your target at month 6 is 1,200 boxes, so you are claiming roughly the whole reachable market. Say that honestly, or widen the area

v: Name the source of every count: I counted them on 14 November, or the shopkeeper told me
Round down, never up. A cautious number survives questions
Say what share you expect and why
If you cannot reach the number you need, the plan needs a different area, not a bigger claim

b.v: 2) A competitor table with three rows

Describe three competitors: the big frozen brand, the local halwa puri shop, and the neighbour who makes samosas on order. Then say what each does better than you, out loud. That honesty is what makes the rest believable.

v: Big frozen brand = cheaper per piece, available everywhere, but tastes factory-made and has no chicken-filling option
Local shop = fresh daily, customers trust them, but no home delivery and closed in the evening
Home cook nearby = very cheap, but inconsistent and takes large orders only with two days notice
Your position = fresh-tasting, consistent, delivered to the shop before 10 am, six days a week

b.v: Do not write that you have no competition. Every customer is already buying something, even if it is making samosas at home. A plan with no competitors tells the reader you have not looked, and they will assume you have not looked at the numbers either.
3) One advantage, stated plainly
Most small businesses have one real advantage, not five. Find it and repeat it everywhere. If you claim five, the reader believes none.

v: Weak = we use the best ingredients and give the best service
Strong = we deliver before 10 am, six days a week, and shops get the same taste every time
Test = could a competitor copy it in a month? If yes, it is not an advantage, it is a feature
Keep = the advantage that comes from something hard to copy: your location, your recipe, your relationship with 40 shopkeepers

b.v: Practice

Count real customers this week: walk or call and count shops in your two best areas. Write the bottom-up number with the date you counted. Then write the three-competitor table including what each does better than you.

day-4.t: Day 4 — The revenue model in rupees

b.v: Today's goal

v: Name every way money comes in, and the main one
Set a price with a reason
Build a month-by-month volume ramp that you can defend

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write your prices on paper first, before the spreadsheet.

A revenue model is simply who pays, how much, how often, and why they keep paying. Most small plans fail here because they list one line called sales with a number that appeared from hope. Break it into units and the whole plan becomes checkable.
1) List the streams, then choose one
You can have several streams, but one should carry most of the money. If three streams each carry a third, you probably have three half-businesses.

v: Main stream = wholesale boxes to shops. Target 80 per cent of revenue
Second stream = home delivery orders through WhatsApp. Higher price per box, more effort
Third stream = bulk orders for events and offices. Few, large, and useful in Ramadan
Rule = if a stream is under 5 per cent of revenue, either grow it deliberately or drop it from the plan

b.v: 2) Price with a reason, not a guess
Three pricing inputs matter: what the customer pays today, what your cost allows, and what your position justifies. Write all three, then choose.

Set the price for one box of 20 samosas:|What shops pay today for a similar box from the big brand: Rs 470|Your cost to make and deliver: Rs 310|The premium your freshness and 10 am delivery justifies: about Rs 50|Chosen price: Rs 520 to shops, Rs 590 for home delivery including delivery|What you give up: you will lose the cheapest buyers, and that is deliberate

v: Home delivery costs more to serve, so it must cost the customer more
Never price below cost to win a shop. You will be busy and poor
Write the price in the plan exactly. A range like Rs 500 to 600 tells the reader you have not decided

b.v: Do not build the plan on a price increase later. If the plan only works after you raise prices by 20 per cent next year, the plan does not work. Show the profit at today's price, then mention the increase as an upside, not a requirement.
3) A volume ramp you can defend
Volume does not jump. It starts from what you sell now and grows by named actions. Each month's number should have a reason attached, such as five new shops.

v: Month 1 = 600 boxes, from the 6 shops you already supply plus home orders
Month 3 = 900 boxes, from 12 shops. Two new shops a month is one morning of visits a week
Month 6 = 1,200 boxes, from 18 shops plus 60 regular homes
Month 12 = 1,500 boxes, from 22 shops plus homes. Still below the 1,180 reachable wholesale boxes plus homes
Every step = tied to a countable action, never to hope

b.v: Practice

Write your streams, pick the main one, and set one price with the three inputs written down. Then write the boxes or units you will sell in months 1, 3, 6 and 12, with the action that gets you there. If a number has no action, remove it.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Unit economics: does one sale make money?

b.v: Today's goal

v: Calculate contribution per unit correctly
Separate direct costs from fixed costs
Spot the unit that loses money at any volume

b.v: About 25 minutes. A calculator is enough. This is the most important page in the plan.

Unit economics means: when I sell one more unit, how much money is left after the costs that unit causes? That leftover is called contribution, and it is what pays rent, salaries and you. If contribution is negative, selling more makes you poorer faster.
1) Build the per-box calculation
Include only costs that change when you make one more box. Rent and salaries do not belong here, because they do not change with one extra box.

v.cap: Unit economics for one box of 20 samosas

v: Direct cost = Rs 310 per box
Contribution = Rs 520 − Rs 310 = Rs 210 per box
Margin = 210 ÷ 520 = 40 per cent, roughly
Meaning = every box sold puts Rs 210 towards rent, salaries and profit

b.v: 2) Direct costs versus fixed costs

The test is one question: if I sell nothing this month, do I still pay this? If yes, it is fixed. If no, it is direct. Getting this wrong is the single most common reason a plan looks profitable and the bank account is empty.

v: Direct = ingredients, packaging, gas, delivery, payment charges on each order
Fixed = rent, staff salaries, internet, marketing retainer, bike instalment, owner draw
Mixed = electricity. Split it: the production part is direct, the shop lights part is fixed
Never put a fixed cost into the unit price. You will underprice and never notice

b.v: Do not forget the costs that arrive monthly but feel invisible: gas cylinder refills, bike servicing, phone bills, wastage. A plan that ignores 8 per cent wastage on a food product is out by that much on every single box.
3) Test a second product before you add it
The same sum tells you whether a new item is worth making. Many small businesses add a product that sells well and earns nothing.

Test the paratha pack:|Price to shops: Rs 380 for 10 parathas|Direct cost: flour, ghee, packaging, gas, delivery = Rs 300|Contribution: Rs 80 per pack, a 21 per cent margin|Compare: samosa box earns Rs 210 for similar effort and freezer space|Decision: sell parathas only where they increase the shop's total order, not as a main line
Practice

Build the per-unit table for your main product on paper. Then add the second product or service you are considering and compare contribution per unit of effort. Decide which one deserves your freezer space, your shelf, or your evening.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Cost structure and what you must pay every month

b.v: Today's goal

v: List every fixed cost honestly, including your own salary
Add the one-off setup costs separately
Find the three costs that decide whether you survive

b.v: About 20 minutes. Open your last three months of spending, if you have them.

Fixed costs are the floor under your business. They must be paid whether you sell ten boxes or a thousand, which is why a long list of small monthly commitments is more dangerous than one large one. Write them all down, then ask which ones you could switch off in a bad month.
1) The monthly fixed cost list
Put your own pay in this list. A plan where the owner works for free is not a business plan, it is a hobby with a spreadsheet. If the business cannot pay you, say so and say when it will.

v.cap: Monthly fixed costs for Sana's Kitchen

v: Total fixed = Rs 2,02,000 per month
That is Rs 2,02,000 ÷ 30 = about Rs 6,733 every single day, sold or not
Owner draw is a real cost. Remove it and you will quietly work for nothing for a year
Any cost you can cancel with one phone call is flexible. Keep as many of those as possible

b.v: 2) One-off setup costs are not monthly costs
A freezer is bought once and lasts years. Putting it in the monthly cost list distorts everything. Keep a separate setup list, funded from the money you are asking for.

v: Blast freezer = Rs 4,50,000
Delivery bike = Rs 3,20,000
Packaging stock, deposits, licences and initial marketing = Rs 1,30,000
Working capital for the loss-making first months = Rs 6,00,000

b.v: Do not use the investment to pay monthly bills in month one. If working capital is being spent on rent on day three, either the numbers are wrong or the business is too small for the freezer you bought. Split the money by purpose and track it.
3) Find your three dangerous costs
Not all costs are equal. Three of them decide whether a bad month kills you. Know them by name and check them every week.

Identify yours:|The largest fixed cost. For Sana it is rent plus staff, Rs 1,14,000|The cost that jumps suddenly. Ingredients during a vegetable price spike|The cost with a penalty attached. A bike instalment or a late rent payment|For each: write the early warning sign and the action you would take
Practice

Write your full monthly fixed cost list including your own pay, and add it up. Then divide by 30 to get your daily cost of existing. Write that number on a card and stick it where you work. It changes how you think about a slow Tuesday.

day-7.t: Day 7 — A 12-month cash flow you can build in an hour

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a 12-month cash flow with five columns only
Separate cash from profit
Find the month where cash hits its lowest point

b.v: About 25 minutes. Do it in a spreadsheet, not in your head.

Profit is an opinion about a period. Cash is a fact about a day. Businesses fail with a profitable plan because the cash ran out in month three while customers paid in month five. The cash flow statement is the one page a lender always looks at twice.
1) Five columns, twelve rows
Keep it this simple or you will not maintain it. Cash in means money that actually arrived, not invoices sent.

v: Month = 1 to 12
Cash in = money received from sales, plus any loan or investment in that month
Cash out = direct costs plus fixed costs, paid in that month
Net = cash in minus cash out
Closing balance = last month's closing balance plus this month's net

b.v: 2) The worked table

Sana starts with Rs 6,00,000 of working capital, after the freezer and bike are already bought. Sales are collected in the same month. Direct cost is Rs 310 a box and fixed cost is Rs 2,02,000 a month.

v: Check month 1 by hand: 600 boxes × Rs 520 = Rs 3,12,000 in. Out = 600 × 310 = 1,86,000 plus 2,02,000 fixed = Rs 3,88,000. Net = −Rs 76,000
Year total = the closing balance of Rs 10,74,000 minus the opening Rs 6,00,000 = Rs 4,74,000 generated
Lowest point = month 3, at Rs 4,66,500. That is your cash trough

b.v: Do not assume customers pay on time. If shops pay after 30 days, month 1 cash in is zero and the trough is deeper and later. Add one column for receivables and test the plan with a 30-day delay before you take anyone's money.
3) Read the trough, not the last line
A plan that ends the year with a big balance can still be dead in month three. The number that matters is the lowest closing balance, because that is the moment you run out if anything goes wrong.

v: Trough = Rs 4,66,500 in month 3. That is comfortable, so the plan survives
If the trough were near zero, you would need more working capital or a slower buying plan
Add a stress test: what if sales are 20 per cent lower for the first three months?
Stress trough for Sana = about Rs 3,50,000. Still alive, and now you can say so with a number

b.v: Practice

Build the five-column table for your own business with realistic monthly volumes. Check two months by hand. Then find your trough month and write one sentence: if sales are 20 per cent lower than planned, my lowest cash balance would be about Rs ___, which is enough or not enough.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Break-even and how much cushion you have

b.v: Today's goal

v: Calculate break-even in units and in rupees
Work out your safety margin
Use break-even to answer the price question

b.v: About 20 minutes. You need the contribution per unit from Day 5 and fixed costs from Day 6.

Break-even is the sales level where you neither make nor lose money. It is the most useful single number in the plan, because it turns a vague hope into a daily target and tells a lender exactly how much room you have if things go wrong.
1) Two formulas, one idea
Break-even in units equals fixed costs divided by contribution per unit. Break-even in rupees equals fixed costs divided by the contribution margin. Same idea, two shapes.

Calculate for Sana:|Fixed costs: Rs 2,02,000 a month|Contribution per box: Rs 210|Break-even boxes: 202,000 ÷ 210 = 961.9, so 962 boxes a month|Break-even sales in rupees: 962 × 520 = Rs 5,00,240, or about Rs 5,00,000|Break-even per day: 962 ÷ 26 working days = 37 boxes a day

v: At 800 boxes = 800 × 210 = 1,68,000 contribution, so a loss of Rs 34,000
At 962 boxes = 962 × 210 = 2,02,020 contribution, so roughly zero. That is break-even
At 1,200 boxes = 2,52,000 contribution, so Rs 50,000 profit
The gap between 962 and 1,200 is your cushion. Protect it

b.v: 2) Safety margin in one line
Safety margin tells you how far sales can fall before you lose money. It is the sentence that makes a lender relax.

v: Formula = (planned sales − break-even sales) ÷ planned sales
Meaning = sales can fall by almost a third and you still break even
Under 15 per cent = thin. Either raise price, cut fixed costs, or plan a bigger volume

b.v: Do not drop your price to reach break-even volume faster. A lower price reduces contribution per box, which pushes break-even higher, so you have to sell even more. Discounting to fix a volume problem usually makes it worse.
3) Use the number every week
Break-even is not a one-time calculation. It is a weekly target you can compare with actual sales, which is far more useful than a monthly surprise.

Put it to work:|Write the weekly break-even: 962 ÷ 4.3 = about 224 boxes a week|Each Sunday, compare actual boxes sold with 224|If you are below for two weeks running, act on cost or price, not on hope|Recalculate break-even whenever rent, salary or price changes
Practice

Calculate your break-even in units, in rupees and per day. Then calculate your safety margin at your planned volume. If it is under 15 per cent, write the two changes you could make this month to widen it.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Risks, the ask, and the use of funds

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write the four risks a reader is already thinking about
State the ask as an exact number with a purpose for every rupee
Say how and when the money comes back

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write the section a nervous lender would write about you.

The risks page is where most plans get weaker, because writers either hide risks or list silly ones like power failure. A good risks page names the four things that would actually hurt, gives each a response, and makes the reader feel that you have already thought about the worst month.
1) Four risks with real responses
For each risk, write the risk, the early warning sign, and the response. If a risk has no response, say what you would do to limit the damage instead of pretending it will not happen.

v: Demand lower than planned = warning is under 962 boxes for two weeks. Response: push home delivery, which earns Rs 70 more per box, and pause the third staff hire
Ingredient price rise = warning is a 15 per cent rise in chicken or flour. Response: re-cost the box and raise the shop price by Rs 20, or reduce the piece size visibly rather than quietly
A key shop stops ordering = warning is one shop skipping two weeks. Response: keep no single shop above 15 per cent of revenue
Freezer breakdown = warning is any temperature alarm. Response: service contract, and a written arrangement with a nearby kitchen for emergency storage

b.v: 2) The ask: exact, split, and dated
Never write we need approximately 15 to 20 lakh for expansion. An exact number with a purpose per rupee tells the reader you have done the work, and it makes the decision easy to say yes to.

Write the ask in five lines:|Amount: Rs 15,00,000|Type: Rs 10,00,000 as a loan over 36 months, Rs 5,00,000 as equity, or the whole amount as a loan. Choose one and say why|Use: blast freezer Rs 4,50,000, delivery bike Rs 3,20,000, packaging and deposits Rs 1,30,000, working capital Rs 6,00,000|Timing: Rs 11,50,000 in month 0, Rs 3,50,000 held for month 2|Repayment: from month 4, when the cash flow turns positive, at Rs ___ per month

v: Every rupee needs a line. A line called miscellaneous tells the reader you are hiding something
If you already own something and are counting it, say so and give it a value
Say what you will NOT spend it on. Freezer money will not pay rent
Keep a simple record of spending against each line, and offer to show it monthly

b.v: Do not promise a repayment schedule the cash flow cannot support. If month 3 is your cash trough, a repayment starting in month 2 is a promise you will break. Read the trough month first, then set the first repayment after it.
3) Say what could make you fail, in one paragraph
One short, honest paragraph near the end does more for credibility than another chart. It shows judgement, and it prepares the reader for a conversation instead of a shock.

v: Name the single biggest reason this could fail
Say what you would do in the first month you saw it happening
Say what you would give up first: the bike, the second staff member, the home delivery line
Never write that failure is not an option. It reads as naive

b.v: Practice

Write your four risks with warning signs and responses, then the five-line ask with an exact rupee amount per line. Add up the lines and confirm they equal the total. If they do not, fix the numbers before anyone sees the page.

day-10.t: Day 10 — The pitch deck and the ten-minute conversation

b.v: Today's goal

v: Turn the plan into ten slides
Deliver a 90-second version without notes
Handle the four questions that always come

b.v: About 20 minutes. Practise out loud, once, even alone.

The plan is read alone. The deck is presented to a face. They do different jobs: the plan proves you have thought it through, the deck makes the reader want to open the plan. Ten slides and ninety seconds are enough for both.
1) Ten slides, in this order
One idea per slide, one number per slide, and never more than 20 words on a slide. If you need more words, you need another slide or you need to talk.

v: 1 Title and one line = what it is and who it is for
2 The problem = what customers do today and why it annoys them
3 The product = a photo of the actual box, not a stock image
4 The customer = who buys, how often, and the 11 shops reordering now
5 The market = the bottom-up count, with your reachable share
6 Unit economics = Rs 520 price, Rs 310 cost, Rs 210 contribution
7 Traction = current monthly boxes and revenue, honestly
8 The plan = volume ramp for 12 months, one line on the chart
9 The ask = Rs 15,00,000 and the four uses
10 The team and the risk = who is doing this, and the one thing that could go wrong

b.v: 2) The 90-second version
You will be asked what do you do in a corridor, in a lift, or at a wedding. If you cannot answer in 90 seconds, you do not yet have the plan in your head.

Say it in this shape:|We make frozen samosas and parathas in Lahore and deliver to shops before 10 am|Shops currently buy a cheaper frozen brand that customers say tastes factory-made|Each box sells at Rs 520 and costs Rs 310, so we keep Rs 210|We sell 1,200 boxes a month now and need 962 to break even|We are asking for Rs 15,00,000 for a blast freezer, a bike and working capital, repaid over three years from month four
Do not open with your life story. The reader did not ask how you started cooking in 2019. Open with what you sell and to whom, and let them ask about the story if they want it.
3) The four questions that always come
Prepare these before the meeting, and answer with a number, not a feeling. A confident number is more persuasive than a long explanation.

v: What if sales are half your plan? Answer with the trough: at 600 boxes we lose Rs 76,000 a month, and our cash lasts five months at that rate, so we would cut the second staff member in month two
Why will shops switch? Answer with the 11 that already reorder and the delivery time, not with taste adjectives
What is your own salary? Answer with the exact figure and when it starts
What happens if I say no? Answer honestly: we grow at half the speed, from our own cash, and open the second area next year instead

b.v: Practice

Build the ten slides, put one number on each, and rehearse the 90-second version out loud three times. Then record it on your phone once and listen. You will hear one sentence you can cut and one number you are unsure about. Fix both before the real meeting.
